enonce_markdown: On a geological map of an area of rugged relief, what is the pattern of the boundaries between horizontal beds?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A horizontal bed lies at a constant height, so its boundary on the map is a line of constant height.

### Solution

A boundary between horizontal beds is at the same elevation everywhere, so it is a contour line and the outcrop follows the topographic contours, giving irregular, branching (dendritic) patterns in dissected country. Straight parallel boundaries occur for vertical beds, which are unaffected by the relief.

**Answer: d.**

choix.texte: Straight lines running north to south
Straight parallel lines, whatever the relief
Lines at right angles to the topographic contour lines
Lines that follow the topographic contour lines

enonce_markdown: Define the **strike** and the **dip** of a bed. A bed has a strike of 040 degrees (bearing) and dips at 30 degrees towards the south-east. State the bearing of the direction of dip and explain how you obtained it.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The strike is a horizontal line drawn on the bed. The dip is the greatest angle between the bed and the horizontal, measured at right angles to the strike.

### Solution

- The **strike** is the direction (bearing) of a horizontal line drawn on the surface of an inclined bed.
- The **dip** is the maximum angle of inclination of the bed from the horizontal. It is measured at right angles to the strike, in a vertical plane, and is given with its direction.

The direction of dip is perpendicular to the strike. The perpendiculars to 040 degrees are 130 degrees and 310 degrees. Since the bed dips towards the south-east, the direction of dip is **130 degrees**. The record is: strike 040 degrees, dip 30 degrees towards 130 degrees.

enonce_markdown: On flat ground, a uniformly dipping bed of sandstone outcrops in a band 200 m wide, measured at right angles to the strike. The bed dips at 30 degrees. What is the true (perpendicular) thickness of the bed?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

On level ground the outcrop width w, measured along the direction of dip, is related to the true thickness t by t = w x sin(dip).

### Solution

t = w sin(dip) = 200 x sin 30 degrees = 200 x 0.5 = **100 m**.

The value 173 m uses cos 30 degrees, 231 m divides by cos 30 degrees and 400 m divides by sin 30 degrees: these come from using the wrong trigonometric ratio.

**Answer: a.**

enonce_markdown: On a map, a vertical dyke runs north to south. Where it meets a vertical fault, the dyke is broken. Looking across the fault, the part of the dyke on the far side is displaced 150 m to the right of the near part. There is no vertical displacement. What type of fault is it?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A fault with a purely horizontal displacement is a strike-slip fault. It is dextral when the far side appears displaced to the right as you look across the fault, and sinistral when it appears displaced to the left.

### Solution

The fault and the dyke are both vertical and the displacement is entirely horizontal (150 m), so it is a **strike-slip** fault. Normal and reverse faults involve vertical displacement along an inclined plane and would not produce a sideways shift of a vertical dyke. The far side moved to the right as seen from the near side, so it is **dextral**.

**Answer: b.**

enonce_markdown: A geological map shows three bands of sedimentary rock, which are not overturned and are not faulted. Going from east to west, the bands are shale (350 m wide), sandstone (120 m wide) and limestone (200 m wide). All the beds dip west at 40 degrees. Which is the youngest rock of the three?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

In a sequence which is not overturned, beds are younger in the direction in which they dip.

### Solution

Beds dipping to the west pass below the ground towards the west, and the beds found further west lie above (on top of) the beds further east. By superposition they are younger. The order from oldest to youngest is shale, sandstone, limestone, so the **limestone is the youngest**. The width of a band depends on thickness, dip and the relief, but not on the age.

**Answer: c.**

choix.texte: The sandstone and the limestone are of equal age

enonce_markdown:
On level ground at 300 m above sea level, a bed of sandstone outcrops along a north-south line **A** (the top of the sandstone). The bed dips at 20 degrees to the east. The outcrop is 160 m wide (measured east-west) and the surface is flat. Assume that the dip is constant.

(a) Calculate the true thickness of the sandstone. (b) At a point **B**, 500 m east of the top of the outcrop along A, how deep below the surface is the top of the sandstone, and at what elevation above sea level is it? (c) At what horizontal distance east of A would a vertical borehole reach the top of the sandstone at a depth of 100 m? Give the answers to the nearest metre, or one decimal place where indicated.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

For a uniformly dipping bed under level ground, the depth below the surface at a horizontal distance d from the outcrop along the direction of dip is d x tan(dip). The true thickness is the outcrop width x sin(dip).

### Solution

**(a)** t = 160 x sin 20 degrees = 160 x 0.3420 = **54.7 m** (to 1 decimal place).

**(b)** Depth = 500 x tan 20 degrees = 500 x 0.3640 = **182 m** below the surface. Elevation of the top of the sandstone at B = 300 - 182 = **118 m above sea level**.

**(c)** tan 20 degrees = 100 / d, so d = 100 / 0.3640 = **274.7 m** (to 1 decimal place) east of A.

Checks: the dip is the angle at the outcrop between the horizontal (surface) and the bed, so the depth increases linearly with the distance in the direction of dip. At 274.7 m the depth is 100 m, consistent with 182 m at 500 m (the ratio 0.364).
